evidence.label: An exact Hausdorff gauge for SLE
An explicit exact Hausdorff gauge for SLE

headline: An explicit size rule gives every piece of an SLE random curve a positive, finite Hausdorff measure.
scope: It covers ordinary chordal SLE for every κ between 0 and 8. It does not relate the two exact gauges to each other.
plain: SLE curves are random, very wiggly curves in the plane. Their dimension was known, but the matching power of distance gives them zero size. The papers claim a corrected size rule that gives every piece a positive, finite size, first implicitly and then as a formula. They also show that Schramm's own suggested rule is too large.
doesNot: This does not say how the explicit gauge relates to the first paper's gauge.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Oded Schramm, Hausdorff-measure problem for SLE
scorecard.significanceWhy: It answers Schramm's question with an explicit gauge and rules out his suggested candidate.

explanation:
To measure a smooth curve, cover it with small discs and add up their sizes. A curve of length 1 needs about 1/r discs of width r. Their widths add up to about 1, whatever r is. The power of r that makes the total settle down is the curve's dimension, here 1.

Some random curves are so wiggly that this fails. Schramm–Loewner evolution, or SLE, is a family of random curves in the plane. They describe boundaries in critical models of physics, such as percolation clusters. A parameter κ sets how wiggly the curve is. For κ between 0 and 8, Beffara showed that the dimension is d = 1 + κ/8[1]. So with κ = 4, d = 1.5.

One might then measure the curve with r^1.5 in place of r. Rezaei showed that this gives zero[2]. The pure power is slightly too small. It needs a tiny correction factor, and the full size rule is called a gauge. Schramm asked for a gauge that gives the curve a sensible, nonzero size[3]. He suggested r^d × log log(1/r).

The first paper claims that a suitable gauge exists for every κ between 0 and 8[4]. It gives every piece of the curve a positive, finite size. But the gauge is defined through integrals, and its shape need not be a neat formula[5].

The second paper names the gauge outright. It is h(r) = r^d × (log log(1/r))^((2−d)/2). It claims this gives every positive-time piece of the curve a positive, finite size[6]. The paper calls this an explicit solution to Schramm's problem[7]. The whole curve inside any bounded disc also has finite expected size[8].

Try κ = 4 and r = 10^(−6). Then log(1/r) is about 13.8, and its log is about 2.63. The correction is 2.63^0.25, about 1.27. Schramm's suggestion uses the full 2.63. The ratio of the two corrections is 2.63^(−0.75), about 0.48. At r = 10^(−100), it falls to about 0.28, and it keeps shrinking. So Schramm's gauge grows too fast in the limit. The paper claims it gives no sensible size on any piece of the curve[9].

The obstacle is that both directions need fine control at every scale. A lower bound needs a mass spread on the curve that is never too heavy in any small disc[12]. An upper bound needs covers whose total cost stays small on average[13]. For the lower bound, the paper deletes small squares that hold too much mass. The cost of reaching a square, its mass, and the number of squares balance out exactly[11]. With κ = 4, the exponents 0.5 and 1.5 add to 2, the dimension of the plane.

Other ways to measure SLE exist. The natural parametrization measures the curve along its own path. Holden and Yuan found a different log correction for ordered pieces of the curve. The gauge here belongs to arbitrary covers instead[14]. The argument needs no link to those other measures[15]. How the two exact gauges relate is still open[10].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal version of one direction. For the explicit gauge, it states that every piece of the curve gets positive size, almost surely. The finite upper bound and the first paper's gauge are not in the scope note. No specialist review of these papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. Lean has a formal version only of the positive lower bound for the explicit gauge; no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: Schramm–Loewner evolution: a family of random curves in the plane, set by a parameter κ.
The power of size that makes the total of a fine cover settle to a nonzero, finite value, when one exists.
A size rule h(r) used in place of a pure power of the width r.
The smallest total gauge cost of covers by small sets, in the limit of finer covers.
Splittable into countably many pieces of finite size.
A way to measure an SLE curve along its own path, not by covers.
